x.name: liberal to conservative
x.desc: The main divide in Texas votes. Today it's almost entirely Democrats against Republicans; in the 1990s, when many rural and South Texas Democrats voted conservatively, the parties overlapped much more.

y.name: establishment to anti-establishment
y.desc: The second divide separates members who vote with their chamber's leadership from those who buck it, within both parties. Among House Republicans the top is each era's Speaker's team: Talmadge Heflin and Fred Hill under Craddick, Four Price and Stan Lambert more recently. The bottom is the rebels: the anti-Craddick Republicans of 2007–09 (Tommy Merritt, Delwin Jones), then Jonathan Stickland, Brian Harrison and Andy Hopper. Among Democrats, mavericks like Terry Canales sit lowest. In the Senate the axis separates institutionalists such as Robert Nichols and Charles Schwertner from members such as Mayes Middleton and Sarah Eckhardt.

dims.note: The second dimension earns its place: it cuts the remaining errors noticeably. A third adds about two-thirds as much again, because Texas votes are less one-dimensional than Congress's. But it doesn't have a clear, stable meaning yet, so the maps show the first two. We'll revisit that as older legislatures are added.
